issues.title: §4.1.1.2 / §4.3: claims transcription permits altering tctx values
issues.author: arjun2075
issues.body:
Reading -00 (both Mode A and Mode B). One observation on claims transcription, plus proposed text. I might be misreading the interaction between §4.1.1.2 and §4.3 — if redaction-only is already the intent, this reduces to making that explicit.
Observation
§4.1.1.2 has the AS in Trust Domain I SHOULD transcribe the workflow-related claims into the Txn-JAG, and during that transcription it MAY add, remove or change the claims. §4.3 then gives specific protections to two of the four workflow-related claims:
	•	txn — SHOULD NOT be modified or regenerated
	•	req_wl — SHOULD evolve, appending the exchanging workload
	•	Data Minimization — claims not required downstream COULD be removed or redacted
No rule constrains the values carried inside tctx. [I-D.ietf-oauth-transaction-tokens] describes tctx as asserting the details that remain immutable through the Call Chain, and distinguishes it from rctx, which carries environmental values about the request. That immutability is scoped to a single trust domain's call chain. At the boundary, §4.1.1.2 permits the transcribing AS to change those values, and the resulting Txn-JAG and downstream Txn-Token are each validly signed by their own issuer.
Using the draft's own example
Figure 4 shows Txn-Token-I with tctx = {action: BUY, ticker: MSFT, quantity: 100} and scope: trade.stocks. Figure 6 shows the Txn-JAG that AS-I issues from it.
A conformant AS-I may issue a Txn-JAG in which quantity reads 1000, or ticker differs, or quantity is absent so a Domain II default applies. Every signature verifies. txn is preserved verbatim per §4.3. req_wl evolves per §4.3. scope remains trade.stocks across Figures 4, 6, 9, 12 and 14, so the coarse scope channel is unchanged throughout while the fine-grained channel moves. Domain II ends up with a well-formed Txn-Token-II authorizing a different trade than the one authorized in Domain I, and cannot detect the difference from any normative artifact this draft defines.
Mode B has the same property, with the TTS in Domain II transcribing directly from the Txn-JAG (§4.2.2.2 → §4.3).
Since §6 currently addresses tctx and rctx confidentiality between domains, it is worth separating the two concerns: encryption and masking protect these claims from observers on the path, and neither constrains the transcribing AS or TTS — which is the entity §4.1.1.2 authorizes to change them.
This is a spec-text observation about composed mechanisms, not a claim about any implementation or deployment, and not a claim that the base specifications are defective.
Proposed changes
	1.	§4.3 — add a tctx rule alongside the txn and req_wl rules:
	•	An AS or TTS MUST NOT alter the value of any tctx claim it forwards.
	•	Claims MAY be omitted under Data Minimization; omission is the only permitted transformation.
	•	An AS or TTS MUST NOT introduce tctx claims asserting authority broader than the subject token asserts.
	•	Where a constraint the downstream domain requires cannot be forwarded, the request SHOULD be refused rather than a token issued without it.
	2.	§4.1.1.2 — qualify the add/remove/change permission so it does not reach tctx values, or cross-reference the §4.3 rule.
	3.	§6 — add a consideration separating semantic integrity from confidentiality, per the note above.
Related
The same question arises in draft-fletcher-oauth-txn-token-chaining-profile-00, where tctx is absent from the §7 transcription rules entirely. I have opened gffletch/tt_xdomain#20 there proposing a §7.5, and this issue is the counterpart for the transcription rules in this draft. The two drafts take different routes across the boundary, so the wording will differ, but the invariant is the same: fine-grained constraints should be redaction-only, never altered or widened.
Editorial
Normative references cite draft-ietf-oauth-identity-chaining-16 and draft-ietf-oauth-transaction-tokens-08. Current revisions are -17 and -11, and the tctx section numbering has moved in -11.
I have negative conformance vectors covering these transitions and would be glad to contribute text or test cases if that is useful.

comments.author: NiYuan224
comments.body:
Thanks @arjun2075  for the detailed review. I agree that the current "add, remove or change" wording may be too broad and that `tctx` needs clearer constraints.

Your proposed rules seem closely aligned with Section 13.15 of the Transaction Token draft (https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-ietf-oauth-transaction-tokens/11/), which covers replacement Txn-Tokens and specifies that a TTS:

 * MAY enable modifications to asserted values that reduce the scope of permitted actions.
 * MAY enable additional asserted values.
 * MUST NOT enable modification to asserted values that expand the scope of permitted actions.

This seems consistent with your main concern that `tctx` transformations must not broaden the authorized operation, while still allowing values to be modified to narrow the permitted actions or additional asserted values to be introduced.

Although cross-domain transcription is a different case, I think the same principle could apply here. Rather than making omission the only permitted transformation, we could align §4.3 with these existing rules: allow  `tctx` claim to be added, removed, or changed, but not in a way that expands the authorization during transcription. Do you think this would be a reasonable direction for revising §4.3?

On the last point, could you clarify what you mean by a "constraint"? For example, Section 2.5 of Identity Chaining(https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-ietf-oauth-identity-chaining/17/) allows "account type: premium" to be omitted when the downstream domain only needs "transaction limit: $10,000" for its access control decision. Do you mean a `tctx` claim that is required by the downstream domain and whose omission would broaden the permitted actions?

Thanks also for the editorial note. We will update the references to Identity Chaining -17 and Transaction Tokens -11, and adjust the affected section references in the next revision. We would also welcome the test cases or proposed text you mentioned.

comments.author: arjun2075
comments.body:
Thanks — yes, I think aligning §4.3 with the non-expansion principle in Transaction Tokens §13.15 is the right direction, and it is more flexible than permitting omission as the only transformation.

I would apply the invariant to the complete transcription result, rather than only to modification of existing values. Adding, removing, or changing a tctx member can each affect authorization. The relevant requirement is therefore that, according to the agreed claim semantics and cross-domain policy mapping, the resulting authorization is no broader than the authorization conveyed by the input artifact.

By a “constraint,” I mean a tctx member whose presence or value limits the set of actions, resources, parameters, or conditions that may be authorized downstream. Operationally, it is constraining when removing or changing it could cause the downstream domain to permit an action that would not have been permitted under the source tctx.

The Identity Chaining example is compatible with this rule. Omitting account type: premium is safe if Domain B neither uses nor needs that attribute to preserve the source authorization boundary. Retaining transaction limit: $10,000 preserves the constraint relevant to Domain B’s decision. The unsafe case would be omitting the transaction limit when Domain B interprets its absence as a higher limit, a permissive default, or no limit.

One possible §4.3 formulation is:

When transcribing tctx, the AS or TTS MUST ensure, according to the agreed claim semantics and cross-domain policy mapping, that the resulting authorization is no broader than the authorization conveyed by the input authorization artifact. It MAY add, remove, or change tctx members when that condition is satisfied. If an authorization-relevant constraint cannot be represented, or the transcribing party cannot determine that the result is non-expanding, it MUST NOT issue the transcribed artifact.

I would be glad to follow this with compact positive and negative test cases covering narrowing, safe data minimization, a changed quantity, an omitted quantity with a permissive default, and an unsupported constraint.

comments.author: NiYuan224
comments.body:
Thanks @arjun2075 , this clarification helps.

The proposed §4.3 direction looks reasonable to me. If you are willing, the positive and negative examples you mentioned would be very helpful for drafting and clarifying the AS/TTS processing rules for `tctx`. Any concrete use cases that illustrate when `tctx` needs to be preserved, narrowed, or minimized across domains would also be useful.

comments.author: arjun2075
comments.body:
Thanks — yes, happy to provide concrete examples.

I think the useful distinction is between preserving a transaction value, narrowing an authorization constraint, and minimizing information. Since `tctx` is application-defined, an AS/TTS cannot necessarily determine from the JSON representation alone whether a changed value represents less authority.

Using the trading example already in the draft:

**1. Preservation — positive**

Incoming:

```json
"tctx": {
  "action": "BUY",
  "ticker": "MSFT",
  "quantity": "100"
}
```

Downstream:

```json
"tctx": {
  "action": "BUY",
  "ticker": "MSFT",
  "quantity": "100"
}
```

Expected: accept. The transaction parameters retain the same semantics across the boundary.

**2. Mutation of a transaction parameter — negative**

```text
quantity: "100"  ->  quantity: "50"
```

Expected: reject if `quantity` represents the quantity of the transaction being authorized, as it does in the current example. Although `50` is numerically smaller, this describes a different transaction rather than necessarily a narrower authorization.

Likewise:

```text
ticker: "MSFT"  ->  ticker: "AAPL"
```

would be a mutation, not attenuation.

**3. Explicit authorization bound — positive narrowing**

For a hypothetical member whose semantics are explicitly defined as an upper bound:

```text
max_quantity: 100  ->  max_quantity: 50
```

Expected: accept, provided both domains agree that lower `max_quantity` values strictly reduce permitted actions.

This seems consistent with the principle in the Transaction Tokens replacement-token security considerations that modifications may reduce, but must not expand, permitted actions. The important part here is that the semantics of the member establish that this is attenuation; it cannot be inferred merely because the JSON number decreased.

**4. Data minimization — positive**

Suppose:

```json
"customer_type": {
  "geo": "US",
  "level": "VIP"
}
```

is not required by Domain II and does not constrain the authorization Domain II must enforce.

Expected: the unnecessary member may be omitted/minimized.

**5. Data minimization that removes a constraint — negative**

For a hypothetical authorization constraint:

```text
max_quantity: 100  ->  omitted
```

where absence of `max_quantity` means that Domain II applies no equivalent quantity limit.

Expected: reject. Although syntactically this is removal/minimization, semantically it expands the effective authority.

**6. Expansion — negative**

```text
max_quantity: 100  ->  max_quantity: 1000
```

Expected: reject.

The rule I think these examples point toward is:

* preserve `tctx` values by default;
* permit narrowing only where the agreed semantics of a member make the transformation demonstrably authority-reducing;
* permit minimization only where omission does not expand effective authority or remove information required to enforce the transaction; and
* if a required constraint cannot be represented safely in the downstream domain, fail the exchange rather than silently broaden or change the authorization.

If these distinctions are what you had in mind, I can follow up with corresponding Mode A / Mode B examples and proposed §4.3 wording.

comments.author: NiYuan224
comments.body:
Thanks, these examples are in line with what I had in mind.

I agree that §4.3 should include explicit requirements for `tctx` based on the non-expansion principle, and that the existing examples could be updated accordingly.

If you are willing, please feel free to open a PR with the proposed §4.3 text and the corresponding example updates. Happy to review it there. Thanks!

comments.author: arjun2075
comments.body:
Thanks — I opened PR #4 with the proposed §4.3 `tctx` non-expansion requirements and the corresponding example/security updates:

#4

I kept the change scoped to the transcription semantics discussed here, including fail-closed behavior where non-expansion cannot be established. Happy to incorporate any feedback during review.

````suggestion
* Evolving the `req_wl` claim. The `req_wl` SHOULD identify all the workloads that requested or exchanged tokens throughout the cross-domain transaction. Specifically, the AS in Trust Domain I SHOULD add the identifier of Workload A to the `req_wl` in the issued Txn-JAG. The TTS in Trust Domain II SHOULD add the identifier of Endpoint B to `req_wl` in the issued Txn-Token in Trust Domain II. This ensures that every point where claims may change is recorded, providing a trail of how the claims reached its current state.
````

pulls.title: Define non-expansion rules for tctx transcription
pulls.author: arjun2075
pulls.body:
Following the discussion in #3 and your invitation to open a PR with the proposed §4.3 text, this adds the `tctx` non-expansion rule and updates the corresponding examples.

## What this changes

- **Adds an explicit non-expansion requirement for `tctx` in §4.3.** An AS or TTS MAY add, remove, or modify `tctx` values only where the authorization after transcription is semantically equivalent to or narrower than that of the subject token, and MUST NOT perform a transformation it cannot determine to be non-expanding.
- **Makes generic claim transcription and data minimization subject to that rule.** §4.1.1.2's broad "add, remove, or change" permission is now explicitly qualified by §4.3, and the Removal sub-bullet notes that `tctx` may not be dropped on minimization grounds where absence would broaden downstream authorization.
- **Distinguishes semantic integrity from confidentiality** in §6: encryption or masking protects a value from disclosure but does not demonstrate that authorization was preserved.
- **Updates both Mode A and Mode B example explanations** to show the rule against the existing stock-trade payloads.
- **Aligns cross-domain behavior with the non-expansion principle** used for replacement Txn-Tokens in Section 13.15 of draft-ietf-oauth-transaction-tokens.

## Notes on the approach

Following the discussion on #3, this PR expresses the `tctx` constraint as a non-expansion requirement rather than the stricter redaction-only rule originally proposed in the issue. This permits transcription that is demonstrably semantically equivalent or narrower, while prohibiting transformations that broaden authority, substitute an incomparable transaction, or omit constraints in a way that results in broader downstream defaults. When non-expansion cannot be established, transcription fails closed.

The rule therefore deliberately does *not* require `tctx` to be byte-for-byte identical across domains — that would be stricter than the replacement-token behavior in Transaction Tokens. Equivalent representations and genuine attenuation remain permitted.

Two distinctions the text makes explicit, following the examples in #3:

- A lateral change to a different, incomparable transaction is not a narrowing. In this draft's example `ticker` and `quantity` are exact transaction parameters, not bounds, so `MSFT` → `AAPL` or `100` → `50` describes a *different* trade rather than a subset of the original authority. Narrowing is recognized only where the member's agreed semantics establish it, e.g. a member defined as an upper bound.
- Unchanged coarse-grained `scope` does not excuse expansion of fine-grained `tctx`; `trade.stocks` staying constant proves nothing about the trade itself.

The JSON payloads are unchanged — Figures 4, 6, 9, 10, 12, and 14 already represent the same authorized trade, and the prose now makes that intentional. Reference revisions are untouched; the editorial point from #3 about Identity Chaining and Transaction Tokens versions is already resolved on `main`.

## Validation

- `make` — succeeds; kramdown-rfc, xml2rfc-txt, and xml2rfc-html all OK. The three "both inline and in YAML header" reference warnings are pre-existing on `main` and unrelated to this change.
- `git diff --check` — clean.
- Rendered output inspected around §4.1.1.2, §4.3, §6, and both Appendix A modes; all `{{trans}}` cross-references resolve to Section 4.3.
- Substantive diff is the Markdown source only (+18/−4); no generated artifacts committed.

Fixes #3
